problem: A fixed-vocabulary speech model must be retrained when users add new words, especially in languages with little labeled data.
contribution: PLiX trains prototypical audio models across many words and languages so new vocabularies can be specified by a few support clips without updating the encoder.
reading_guide: Recognition is evaluated through closed-set few-shot episodes; the numeric tables below measure only encoder latency and energy.

diagram.title: Recognize a new vocabulary
diagram.description: At inference, labeled support clips and query audio share an encoder. Only support embeddings are averaged into word prototypes; query embeddings are compared directly with those prototypes.

stages.title: Support and queries
stages.detail: Provide labeled examples of each word and the audio clips to classify.

stages.title: Shared encoder
stages.detail: Convert clips to log-mel spectrograms and embed both sets with the same trained acoustic model.

stages.title: Support prototypes
stages.detail: Average support embeddings per word; retain each query embedding separately.

stages.title: Nearest word
stages.detail: Compare each query with all prototypes using squared Euclidean distance.

diagram.footnote: This depicts inference after episodic training. Query embeddings are not averaged into prototypes. Predictions choose among the supplied vocabulary; no encoder retraining is required.

results.title: Recognizing new words and languages
results.question: What does the few-shot recognition evaluation demonstrate?
results.context: Qualitative reading of the recognition figures, not values estimated from bar heights. Held-out-word tests use closed-set MSWC episodes; transfer tests use five unseen MSWC languages and FLEURS. Accuracy is averaged over 1,000 episodes without plotted uncertainty intervals.

rows.label: Multilingual base · held-out words
values: Recognizes new words with one support clip; accuracy varies by language and improves with more support.

rows.label: English base · larger vocabulary
values: More competing words reduce one-shot accuracy; more support clips improve recognition.

rows.label: Multilingual base · unseen languages
values: Transfers without retraining to five languages; Tamil is the most difficult in the reported one-shot test.

rows.label: Multilingual base · language identification
values: Transfers to FLEURS without retraining; the ten-language episodes are harder than the smaller tasks.

results.interpretation: Support examples let the same encoder handle a new vocabulary or task, but recognition quality depends on the number of choices, support count and language.
results.caveat: These are qualitative observations from separate experiments, not a pooled performance comparison. English-only and multilingual encoders have different training data. FLEURS contains 102 languages, but each reported episode distinguishes only 3, 5 or 10 languages.

results.title: Encoder latency
results.question: How do encoder size and quantization change inference time on the measured devices?
results.context: TinyNet-E (“Small”) and EfficientNet-v2 Medium (“Base”); average over 200 inference runs. Latency in milliseconds, lower is better; no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: The small encoder is faster on every measured platform, and quantization substantially reduces latency on Raspberry Pi and Jetson Nano.
results.caveat: Encoder-only timings exclude log-mel computation and the prototype classifier. Pixel 7 was tested only with quantized models; accuracy after quantization is not reported here.

results.title: Encoder energy
results.question: Do lower-cost encoders also consume less energy per inference?
results.context: Same encoders and device configurations as the latency panel; average over 200 inference runs measured with an external power monitor. Energy in millijoules, lower is better; no dispersion reported.
results.interpretation: The small encoder uses less measured energy in each configuration; quantized variants reduce energy on both platforms with full-precision comparisons.
results.caveat: These are encoder costs under the reported measurement setup, not whole-application battery consumption or continuous listening cost.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: MSWC: over 12 million one-second clips; 16,665 training and 4,174 test keywords across 20 languages, with disjoint keyword splits.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: EfficientNet-v2 Medium (52.8M parameters) for the base model; TinyNet-E (761,396 parameters) for language-specific small models; ImageNet initialization.

evaluation.label: Transfer
evaluation.value: Five unseen languages: Frisian, Mongolian, Maltese, Slovenian and Tamil; separate few-shot language-identification episodes on FLEURS.

evaluation.label: Protocol
evaluation.value: 1,000 test episodes, normally 15 queries; number of classes and support examples varies. Hardware profiling uses Raspberry Pi 4, Jetson Nano and Pixel 7.

limitations: Recognition results are closed-set episodes over segmented clips; open-set rejection, false-trigger rates and continuous streaming keyword detection are not evaluated.
Generalization varies by language, vocabulary size and support count; the unseen-language experiment covers five languages, not all languages.
Hardware measurements exclude preprocessing and prototype computation, and the paper does not report a corresponding quantized-accuracy comparison.
Recognition accuracy is presented graphically without uncertainty intervals; the small models are trained separately per language and are not the single multilingual base model.
takeaways: New word support clips create new prototypes, so changing the vocabulary does not require fine-tuning.
A single multilingual base model transfers to held-out words and five unseen languages, while additional support examples help harder settings.
The deployment trade-off includes both representation quality and encoder cost; the hardware table alone does not establish end-to-end recognition performance.
